patch.value: The one-release-per-day guard compares a prefix glob against unpadded date keys, so it is correct only by accident of tag creation order and silently skips a real release for any out-of-order tag

The one-release-per-day guarantee is enforced by a string prefix glob over unpadded date keys, so the check does not actually test "was a release cut today". It currently gives the right answer for a reason unrelated to its logic, and this project has already lost a release once to this exact class.

Mechanism, read at HEAD:

- utcDateKey (scripts/release/utils.mjs:67) builds the key from getUTCMonth()+1 and getUTCDate() with NO zero padding, so 1 May is 2026.5.1, not 2026.05.01.
- listTodayTags (scripts/release/run-release-pipeline.mjs:88) runs git tag --list with the pattern v${todayKey}* and treats ANY match as proof that today already has a release.
- maybeSkipForSameDayRelease (:263) then skips the entire pipeline and reports reason release_already_cut_today together with a tags_today list.

The glob is prefix-unsafe for every single-digit day whose number is a prefix of a two-digit day in the same month. Probing the 78 real tags in this repository, 68 derivable day-keys produce 45 cross-day matches: the key 2026.5.1 glob-matches v2026.5.10, v2026.5.11, v2026.5.12, v2026.5.14 and v2026.5.18; 2026.5.2 matches v2026.5.23, .24, .27, .28, .29; 2026.6.1 matches v2026.6.10 through v2026.6.19; and so on. Days 1 to 9 of every month are affected, which is roughly 30 percent of the calendar.

Honest statement of current exposure: under strictly forward-moving time with tags only ever created for the current day, the colliding tags do not exist yet at the moment the guard runs, so no false skip has occurred and today's behaviour is correct - the 2026-07-28 guard matched exactly v2026.7.28. The defect is that this correctness is incidental. The check passes today because of the order in which tags happen to be created, not because the comparison is right.

It becomes a real skipped release the moment any tag exists out of chronological order: a re-cut or re-tag of an earlier day, a hotfix tagged against a prior date, an imported or mirrored tag set, a fork or a clone whose tags arrive in bulk from a fetch, or any repair of the seven tags this project has already declared and never delivered. In each of those cases the guard silently reports release_already_cut_today for a day that has no release, and the pipeline exits reporting ok:true and skipped:true, which is indistinguishable from a healthy no-op.

Precedent that this class is not theoretical here: a padded-versus-unpadded version match previously caused silently skipped releases in this project. The fix then was applied to the matching site that failed. The date-key glob is the same mistake in the sibling site and was not covered.

The correct check is an exact comparison against a parsed tag's own date fields, or a zero-padded canonical key, rather than a prefix glob. The skip decision is also the right place for a negative-control fixture, since a guard that can only be observed skipping correctly is a guard nobody can prove wrong.

Scope is the same-day comparison only. The drifting cron window has its own owner, the scheduled-run failure rate has its own owner, and the three-way divergence between changelog, tags and npm has its own owner. This is none of those: it is whether the comparison that enforces one-release-per-day is testing what it claims.

The same-day release check compares parsed date fields or a zero-padded canonical key rather than a prefix glob, so no tag from a different day can ever satisfy it; A negative-control fixture proves the guard skips when a same-day tag exists and does NOT skip when only a later-day tag from the same month exists; Days 1 through 9 of a month are covered explicitly by regression tests, including the case where a two-digit-day tag from the same month already exists; The skip envelope's tags_today list contains only tags whose own date equals the run's date key; The unpadded date key is either padded canonically or documented as intentional with every consumer audited for prefix-matching

value.text:
First day the collision operand pair actually exists in the tag set. git tag --list "v2026.7.3*" now returns TWO tags: v2026.7.3 (July 3) and v2026.7.30 (July 30). The unpadded utcDateKey plus the v-prefix glob is therefore no longer a hypothetical pairing - the corpus now contains a real tag whose name is a strict prefix of another real tag in the same series.

The honest scope of this item still holds and must not be widened: on 2026-07-03 the key was 2026.7.3 and v2026.7.30 did not yet exist, so the glob could not have matched it; on 2026-07-30 the key is 2026.7.30 and the glob matches only itself. The guard remains correct by accident of forward-moving time, not by logic. What changed today is that the reachability argument no longer needs a hypothetical tag - it needs only a clock that is not monotonic (a re-run against an older ref, a backfilled tag, or a manual dispatch keyed to a past date).

value.text:
Sequencing edge recorded 2026-07-31: this defect is now blocked_by pm-uenmu9 rather than merely adjacent to it.

The reason is that the correct fix is not determined by the defect. The guard compares a prefix glob against unpadded date keys, so it is wrong in a way that has two different correct repairs depending on a policy question nobody has answered: if one release per UTC day is an architectural invariant, the guard should be an exact-match assertion that refuses a second same-day version outright; if a manually triggered same-day release is a supported operation, the guard must distinguish scheduled from dispatched invocations and permit the latter while still refusing an accidental duplicate from the former. Those are different comparisons over different key spaces, and implementing either one before the ruling means implementing it twice.

The workflow already contains a partial answer that the ADR has not ratified. The issues-triggered retry path in .github/workflows/auto-release.yml computes an unpadded today_version, checks git tag --list for an exact v<version> match, and on a hit reruns the existing tag's Release workflow instead of creating a replacement version - with an inline comment stating it never creates a replacement same-day version. So the retry path behaves as though one-per-day is architectural, while the scheduled path's guard lives in run-release-pipeline.mjs and is the one this defect describes. Two paths, one undocumented assumption, no ruling.

This edge makes that dependency traversable instead of leaving it as prose in two separate items.

value.text: Guard re-confirmed live 2026-08-01 at HEAD, with today's date being the case that makes it visible. listTodayTags (scripts/release/run-release-pipeline.mjs:88-89) runs git tag --list "v${todayKey}*" where todayKey comes from utcDateKey (scripts/release/utils.mjs:80-82) and is deliberately unpadded: today it is 2026.8.1, so the glob is v2026.8.1*, which matches v2026.8.1 and would equally match v2026.8.10 through v2026.8.19. The 82 tags in this repository are all v20*-prefixed and were created in chronological order, so no future-dated tag exists to be matched -- which is precisely the accident the item names. The .github/workflows/auto-release.yml same-day retry path at line 163 uses an exact git tag --list "v${today_version}" with no glob, so the two same-day checks in the release path disagree about their own matching rule: one exact, one prefix. Today's observed behaviour was correct: three Auto Release runs (workflow_dispatch 02:23 which published, workflow_dispatch 02:51, schedule 05:41), exactly one tag v2026.8.1, one GitHub release created 02:44:13Z, and npm dist-tags.latest 2026.8.1 modified 02:43:26Z. One release for the day, as intended, by luck of ordering rather than by the guard's construction.
